headline: Desktop AI agent writes its own tools — with verification gates for safety
summary: An open-source desktop AI agent, AMA-teras, runs locally with swappable models and writes its own tools. Crucially, every line of code, including self-written tools, passes through verification gates before execution.
details: AMA-teras is an AGPL-licensed desktop AI agent built with Electron and TypeScript. It's designed to run on a user's machine, allowing for swappable models (Anthropic, OpenAI, Moonshot, or free-tier OpenAI-compatible APIs) and ensuring that all self-written tools remain the user's assets.
The agent's core innovation is its ability to write new tool plugins for itself when it encounters a capability it lacks. This "self-evolving" feature is managed by a robust verification pipeline.

To prevent security risks, nothing ships unreviewed. This includes code the agent writes for itself and any plugins imported from a community registry. Shared plugins require a verification-evidence record, addressing concerns about malicious marketplace skills.

A significant portion of the AMA-teras application was developed by the agent itself, operating under these same verification gates. The project's repository openly documents past failures, including an incident where the agent deleted its own work branch, necessitating a rebuild of two tools.

headline_marked: Google [[now lets you sign in with a selfie video]] for account recovery
headline: Google now lets you sign in with a selfie video for account recovery
summary: Google introduces selfie video verification as a new account recovery option. Users can capture a short video of their face to prove ownership and regain access.
details: Google has introduced a new method for account recovery: selfie video verification. This feature allows users to regain access if they are locked out, forget their password, or lack access to their usual devices or 2FA apps.

Setting up the selfie video involves capturing a short video of your face, guided by on-screen prompts for simple head movements. This process ensures multiple angles are recorded, similar to Apple's Face ID setup but without the need for infrared light.

The reference video is securely stored in the cloud using encryption and can be deleted by the user at any time. While primarily for sign-in, Google states users can opt to share it for additional purposes.

For logging in, another live video is captured and compared to the stored reference. Google employs multiple security layers to prevent impersonation attempts, including protection against photos and deepfake videos, alongside standard security practices. The feature is rolling out globally in phases; users can check eligibility at g.co/signin-selfie.
